definition: Mercurial means marked by rapid, unpredictable changes in mood or behavior.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mercurial. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mercurial should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The band's mercurial drummer could go from laughing at breakfast to storming out of rehearsal by noon.
A moody person slips in and out of low spirits, while a mercurial one swings between entirely different moods with startling speed.
A mercurial temperament changes quickly, but a volatile one goes a step further, ready to erupt at the slightest spark.

Unpredictable means impossible to anticipate from one moment to the next, and it applies to anything - weather, traffic, a bouncing ball. Mercurial is unpredictability located in a person's moods: the swings are rapid and nobody can guess the next one. A schedule can be unpredictable; only a temperament can be mercurial.

Temperamental means prone to sudden shifts of mood, and it carries a note of complaint about machines and divas alike - a temperamental printer, a temperamental soprano. Mercurial keeps the speed but adds range and a certain shimmer: the person swings between entirely different selves, delightful one hour and thunderous the next. Temperamental grumbles; mercurial dazzles and alarms by turns.

The Romans' messenger god Mercury lends his name twice: to the fastest-moving planet and to the liquid metal mercury. Alchemists liked matching metals to the heavens — gold for the sun, silver for the moon — and this restless, silvery metal struck them as belonging to the messenger god: it never stays put.
Mercurial means marked by rapid, unpredictable changes in mood or behavior.
No one on the kitchen staff could predict which version of Chef Alvarez would walk in each morning.
On Monday he praised a line cook's sauce so warmly that she blushed; on Tuesday he sent the very same sauce back three times without explaining why.
By Friday he was cheerfully handing out pastries he had baked at dawn for the whole crew.
The staff learned to read his mercurial moods the way sailors read a changing sky.
The chef's moods shifted quickly and without warning from day to day, which is exactly what mercurial describes.

Ambassadors posted to the court of Elizabeth I filed reports that read like weather logs.
The queen could shower a courtier with gifts in the morning and banish him from her presence before supper, then recall him within the week as though nothing had passed.
Contemporaries called her spirit quicksilver; historians settle for mercurial, and her ministers simply learned to check which way the wind blew before raising delicate business.
Some of it, scholars argue, was strategy: a sovereign no one can read is hard to manipulate.
But her closest advisers, who bore the sudden storms and sudden sunshine for decades, insisted the changes were as real as they were fast.
